Venezuela’s 2021 General Strike Disrupted Key Sectors, Including Oil Giant Petroleos de Venezuela SA

Caracas—Three years after Venezuela’s 2021 nationwide general strike, analysts and industry officials are continuing to assess the event’s impact on the country’s fragile economy, as well as its repercussions for major state-owned enterprises such as Petroleos de Venezuela SA (PDVSA).

The general strike, which began on August 17, 2021, saw workers across a broad range of sectors—including transport, manufacturing, healthcare, and education—walk off the job in protest over wages, working conditions, and government policy. The action lasted four days and brought significant portions of the country’s economic activity to a halt, with major oil installations, ports, and transportation hubs operating at minimum capacity or suspending operations entirely.

PDVSA, Venezuela’s largest employer and the backbone of its export economy, was among the companies most severely affected. According to the Venezuelan Oil Workers Union, over 60% of PDVSA’s workforce participated in the walkout, causing crude oil output to drop by an estimated 22% during the week of the strike. “Operations were severely constrained; some refineries and loading terminals had to scale down or stop altogether,” said union leader Luis Salazar in a recent interview. “The financial losses were significant, not just for PDVSA, but for the nation as a whole.”

The Confederation of Venezuelan Industrialists (CVI) estimated that the strike resulted in a loss of $580 million in industrial output, with ripple effects felt in supply chains and export revenues. “The event underscored the vulnerability of our industrial infrastructure to labor unrest,” said CVI spokesperson Mariana Torres. “Many small and mid-sized firms faced cash shortages and delivery delays that took months to resolve.”

Public transport was another sector hit hard, with the National Federation of Transport Workers reporting that 70% of buses and urban transit services were idled during the strike period. Hospital and school closures added to the disruption, with the Ministry of Health confirming that at least 45% of public clinics operated at emergency staffing levels.

While the strike concluded without major incidents and there have been no comparable disruptions since, its legacy remains in ongoing wage negotiations and government commitments to labor reform. Analysts say the event highlighted the pressing need for social dialogue and economic stabilization in Venezuela. “The 2021 strike was a watershed moment,” said independent economist Javier Montilla. “It forced all parties to confront the deep-seated issues undermining productivity and growth.”
